title: Book 6 — Erato, Chapter 61
paragraphs: Thus are these things done; and at the time of which we speak, while Cleomenes was in Aegina doing deeds which were for the common service of Hellas, Demaratus was bringing charges against him—not so much because he cared about the Aeginetans as because he felt envy and jealousy of him. So Cleomenes, after he returned from Aegina, planned to depose Demaratus from the kingship, making an attempt upon him on the following grounds. Ariston, being king in Sparta and having married two wives, yet had no children born to him; and since he did not acknowledge that he himself was the cause of this, he married a third wife, and married her in this way. He had a friend, a man of the Spartans, to whom of all the citizens Ariston was most attached; and this man happened to have a wife who was by far the fairest of all the women in Sparta, one who had become the fairest after having been the foulest. For since she was ugly in appearance, her nurse, considering that she was the daughter of wealthy parents and was ill-favored in looks, and seeing moreover that her parents were distressed by it, devised the following plan. Every day she would carry her to the temple of Helen, which is at the place called Therapne, lying above the temple of Phoebus; and whenever the nurse carried her there, she would place her before the image and pray to the goddess to deliver the child from her ugliness. Once, as the nurse was leaving the temple, it is said that a woman appeared to her, and having appeared, asked what she was carrying in her arms; and she told her she was carrying a child. At this the other bade her show the child to her, but she refused, for she had been forbidden by the parents to show it to anyone; but the woman kept pressing her to show it. So, perceiving that the woman really wanted to see it, the nurse showed her the child. Then the woman stroked the child's head and said that she would be the fairest of all the women in Sparta; and from that day her appearance was changed. Afterwards, when she came of age, she was married to Agetus son of Alcides, this friend of Ariston of whom we spoke.
